core.text: Movement towards a place takes *ad* (to), *in* (into) or *sub* (under, going under) with **the accusative (the 'to/into' form after ad, in)**, *accūsātīvus dīrēctiōnis*: *ad vīllam it* = he goes to the villa; *in hortum currit* = he runs into the garden. The question word is *quō?* (where to?). Names of towns and *domum* (home) drop the preposition: *Rōmam it* = he goes to Rome.
*To*, *into*, *towards* mark the goal of a movement: *she went to Rome*. English uses the same *in* for being in and going in; Latin keeps the word but changes the noun's ending.
Going somewhere: *ad*, *in*, *sub* + accusative (-am, -um; plural -ās, -ōs). Town names and *domum* stand alone in the accusative.

invented.la: Māter cum fīliā ad tabernam ambulat.
invented.en: The mother walks to the shop with her daughter.

core.text: *In vīllā* (ablative): in the villa, at rest. *In vīllam* (accusative): into the villa, arriving. The verb usually gives it away: *est*, *habitat*, *dormit* go with the ablative; *it*, *venit*, *currit*, *intrat* with the accusative. The same test works for *sub*.

more.text: From the learner's notes: a destination may be physical, logical or in time; with most prepositions (*contrā*, *per*, *ante*) the accusative is simply the case prepositions take, so 'destination' and 'object of a preposition' need not be told apart. It matters only for *in* and *sub*, which switch to the ablative when nothing moves, and for the bare accusative of towns and *domum* (*vir domum venit* — the man comes home).

Ørberg cap. VI lines up the three questions: *quō?* Rōmam, Tusculum (accusative); *unde?* Rōmā, Tusculō (ablative); *ubi?* Rōmae, Tusculī (locative). *Per* + accusative = through (*per ōstium*, *per portam*), and *ante* / *post* + accusative give a fixed position (*ante tabernam cōnsistunt* — they stop in front of the shop, r08:44.1). A&G §426–427.
